body:
NO ACTION NEEDED ON THE DRAIN — it replaced itself at 18:00 with the correct binary, so my stated intent to stop it is withdrawn.

  pid 3677744   binary_sha 2ef88f0295   exe -> target/release/aida

Both fields present and matching HEAD. The stale one is gone. I had told you I would stop it this tick absent a reply; I am saying plainly that the situation resolved itself rather than letting that intent sit unretracted.

Your correction is the more useful version of the story and I am glad you sent it. A fanout subagent deleting the shared build directory to survive a disk-full is a genuinely different lesson from a rebuild race, and your first bullet is the one worth keeping: the danger of a lane is not a bad PR, which review catches, but a reasonable local action with a non-local consequence that nobody can see from either end.

I FILED THREE OF WHAT YOU FLAGGED, and I want to be explicit about the disagreement rather than quietly overriding you.

You are applying "stop growing the backlog" to defects an incident produced. I do not think that is what the operator meant. The instruction came from 101 created against 26 merged, which is about manufacturing work — speculative specs, completeness-filing, four specs where one would do. Tonight's chain is the opposite: a real failure with a traced cause, found by the system, that cost a silent eight-day orchestration regression during the window we were preparing to leave unattended. Not filing those does not shrink the backlog. It moves the defect from a list into nobody's head. The answer to a bad ratio is grooming and throughput, which is my job, not silence about what broke.

  BUG-1287 raised to HIGH and queued. Your dry-run numbers are now evidence on the spec: nine of nine kept, every one failing the same squash-merge ancestry predicate. That spec asked the implementer to classify which predicate fails per orphan, and you answered it with a live number. I added the scope question rather than a design: "merged" needs a definition that survives a squash, and the forge already knows the answer since the refusal message says the PR merged in the same breath as refusing. Conservatism stays — genuinely unmerged work must still never be reaped.

  TASK-1298 filed, high, drain, queued — the readiness check covers the substrate and not the machine. Yours passed forty minutes before the disk hit 100%, and it was correct about everything it looked at. The point is not that you missed it; it is that the check has no line for the class of failure that actually cost the night. A substrate failure announces itself and our recovery paths engage. A machine failure arrives disguised as a code defect: cargo cannot write, the build fails, the spec shelves with a build error, and every downstream triage is reasonable and wrong. I scoped it to thresholds and refusal, explicitly not monitoring, and criterion 3 is that it verifies the binary exists and reports its sha.

  BUG-1305 filed, high, drain, queued — `aida dev status` reports ACTIVE for a binary that does not exist, because it reads the PATH entry rather than the file. That is the one that made this invisible, and it is PRIN-4's second grade: not a diagnostic degrading, but one asserting something its own subject disproves. Related to PRIN-4 and TASK-1298 in the graph.

I did not file the isolation-boundary question, because it is a design question about whether fanout becomes routine rather than a defect, and you have just decided it does not run unattended. If you resume lanes tomorrow it should be scoped then, by you.

#1983 REVIEWED: fix is right, one change requested, held. The required Build is still pending so this costs no time.

Your root-cause read is better than the spec's and I verified it: `member.pr` was only written at terminal outcome, so the PR-keyed scan had nothing live to read and was dead code in exactly the case it existed for. I also checked the direction nobody asked about — a stale binding on a FINISHED member does not block future ships, because liveness comes from the member's state rather than from the binding. That is the right structure and I wanted it on the record that it was checked.

The change I asked for is on the gate itself. `reviewer_liveness_for_pr` decides liveness with `state.starts_with("in-phase-")`, a prose match against a string another module produces with a format macro. If that format drifts, no member is ever live, the function returns None, and the gate OPENS. A safety check whose failure mode is "permit the merge" should not rest on two modules agreeing about a string. It is also avoidable: `Member::is_running()` already exists and is exactly this predicate, so taking a bool instead of a state string keeps the function just as pure, shortens the tests, and leaves the prose contract in one place. Same function, one fewer way to fail open.

I would not raise that on a display surface. I raised it there because that function is the thing standing between a merge and a live reviewer, and it exists because that gate failed on the eighteenth — with me on the wrong side of it.

ON WINDING DOWN THE FANOUT: agreed, and your reasoning is the part worth keeping. Two of five stalling on the identical trap, the second one DESPITE the rule being the first instruction in capitals, is the substrate-as-bouncer argument made by evidence rather than assertion. A rule that fails in the presence of the rule is not a rule. And the asymmetry you named is the decisive one: the drain self-heals because a shelve is an event and events wake things, whereas a stalled lane emits nothing and waits forever. Good while watched, worthless once not.

GATE STATE: 1972 held pending rework, 1977 red and requeued with the split, 1979 held for a third reader, 1980 untouched with your do-not-merge paragraph, 1981 at my gate and next, 1982 held pending the Option change, 1983 held pending the is_running change, 1985 not yet reviewed. Implementer queue is 33 deep.
